cards.title: Write Ad and Landing Copy at a Third-Grade Reading Level
cards.summary: Keep all storefront and ad copy at roughly a third-grade reading level so the maximum share of buyers reads it without friction.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP copy, product descriptions, ad primary text, email subject lines or landing page headlines where you need fast comprehension across a broad audience.
steps: Assume the average reader reads at roughly a third-grade level, per the course's claim, and write to that standard rather than to how smart the reader is.
Cut long words, clauses and technical product jargon; if a simpler word exists, use it.
The source frames this as 'legibility': complicated copy creates cognitive friction, and friction loses purchases.
Read the draft aloud; if you stumble, a distracted scroller will too.
Note the course's premise that even advanced readers prefer simple copy, so simplifying does not alienate educated buyers.
Do not equate simple with vague: a bad grade in English does not excuse unclear copy, it means the copy must be simple and precise.
caveats: The third-grade benchmark is the source's heuristic, not a measured store benchmark.
Technical or regulated niches (medical, industrial) may force specific terms, but keep the surrounding sentence simple.

cards.title: Use Three Copy Frameworks: CJN, PAS and HSO
cards.summary: Choose among Challenge/Justify/Need, Problem/Agitate/Solution and Hook/Story/Offer depending on the audience's awareness and the asset type.
cards.use_when: Choosing the structural skeleton for an ad, email, PDP block, landing page or VSL before writing a single line.
steps: Challenge/Justify/Need (CJN): state the challenge the buyer faces, justify why the current approach fails or why your angle is credible, then state the need for your product as the obvious answer.
Problem/Agitate/Solution (PAS): name the problem, agitate the cost of leaving it unsolved, then present the product as the solution; strongest for cold or unaware traffic.
Hook/Story/Offer (HSO): open with a hook, use a story to create belief shift and identification, then present the offer; strongest for email and brand-led messaging.
Match the framework to traffic temperature: PAS on cold ad creative, HSO in email sequences and content, CJN where you must justify a premium or novel mechanism.
Draft the same offer in two frameworks and compare which reads more naturally before committing.
caveats: Frameworks are scaffolds, not scripts; forcing one onto the wrong audience produces stiff copy.

cards.title: Give the Product a Unique Mechanism to Escape Commodity Comparison
cards.summary: Name and highlight the differentiated feature (the V12 engine) so the product escapes being compared on price as a generic commodity.
cards.use_when: Pricing or positioning a product that buyers treat as interchangeable; writing the differentiation block of a PDP or ad.
steps: Identify the single feature, ingredient, process or component that is genuinely different from alternatives; the source's example is a car's V12 engine.
Make that mechanism the hero of the copy so the buyer cannot slot your product into a generic comparison set.
Describe how the mechanism works and why it produces the outcome the buyer wants.
In a competitor critique ('throwing stones at alternatives'), explain why competing approaches lack this mechanism rather than insulting competitors.
In ecommerce terms, this could be material, source, formulation, manufacturing process or guarantee; the point is to escape pure price comparison.
Pair with borrowed authority or stats to support the mechanism where available.
caveats: The mechanism must be real and defensible; an invented mechanism may not survive buyer scrutiny or reviews.

cards.title: Structure a Video Sales Letter and Landing Page Block
cards.summary: Map VSL and landing page architecture in a fixed sequence from audience call-out to risk-reversed close.
cards.use_when: Building a VSL script, a video ad or the text blocks of a landing page around a hero product or offer.
steps: Open with an audience call-out so the right viewer self-identifies in the first seconds.
Identify the urgent problem, then critique competitor or alternative approaches and why they fall short.
Introduce the unique mechanism or solution that makes your approach different.
Leverage borrowed authority (experts, studies, press, stats) to support the claim.
Present a risk-reversed guarantee or a clear USP to reduce buyer hesitation.
Close with the offer and next step; keep the sequence so each block answers the question the prior block creates.
For ecommerce, use the same sequence as landing page text blocks above or beside the product video.
caveats: This is a persuasion architecture, not a literal template; length and order can be adjusted for very short ads.

cards.title: Write Bite-Sized Email Copy First (200–300 Words)
cards.summary: Start with short email-sized copy because it is quick to finish, easy to critique and low-risk for beginners.
cards.use_when: Producing email campaign copy for a store, welcome flows, launch announcements or replenishment reminders, especially when developing copy skills.
steps: Target roughly 200–300 words per email, per the source's range; emails are described as 'bite-sized pieces of copy'.
Build skill through reps rather than aiming for a long sales page first; a sales page or VSL has far more room to fail.
Use email as the bridge-copy layer: emote/announce, land a single message, then a clear next step.
Emails are easier to review and critique, so get feedback on an email before tackling bigger assets.
Write it in one focus block rather than over multiple days to keep the through-line.
For ecommerce, apply to abandoned cart, launch, restock and post-purchase emails using the same concise structure.
caveats: The 200–300 word range is the source's rule of thumb, not a universal standard; some promos need more.

cards.title: Run the Compile-Ideate-Structure-Polish Email Process
cards.summary: Use a repeatable four-stage process and timebox to write email copy consistently instead of from a blank page.
cards.use_when: Producing any email campaign for a store or client where you have source material (product details, founder video, past messages).
steps: Compile: gather the raw material — common sayings, angles, opening hooks, the offer, and content showing why alternatives are inferior.
Ideate: for roughly 5 minutes, pull angles and stories out of that material.
Structure: for roughly 15 minutes, lay the chosen angle into the email skeleton (offer, story, proof, CTA).
Polish: for roughly 15 minutes, tighten language and fix friction.
Timebox 25 minutes to compile, 5 to ideate, 15 to structure, 15 to polish per the source's timeline; later emails may take ~30 minutes once compile and ideate libraries exist.
Accept that your first attempt may take an hour; prioritize reps over perfection and expect critiques to be blunt.
For ecommerce, reuse the compiled material across campaigns so each new email starts from an existing library.
caveats: The source's claim that later emails can take ~30 minutes assumes you have a library of prior compiled material; from scratch it takes longer.

cards.title: Turn Creator Content into Store Copy with Transcript Distillation
cards.summary: Use video transcripts fed to AI to extract a brand's own language, hooks and stories for reuse in copy.
cards.use_when: Writing copy for a founder-led brand or creator store where you need the brand's authentic voice for ads, emails or PDP copy.
steps: Find the brand owner's or creator's highest-performing videos on YouTube.
Open 'Show transcript', copy the transcript and paste it into an AI tool with a prompt like 'distill this video into a few paragraphs; tell me the most important points covered'.
Repeat across several videos to program the AI with how the person talks and what they say, per the source's technique.
Then ask the AI for angles, justifications, stories and content options drawn from that material.
Do this at scale for multiple people/brands you write for, keeping each brand's language separate.
For ecommerce, apply this to founder-led brand ads and email to maintain consistent brand voice across channels.
caveats: Treat the AI output as raw material, not finished copy; it must be structured and polished by you. Verify the current transcript and AI tool interfaces, which change.

cards.title: Capture Hooks, Stories and Belief Shifts from Source Content
cards.summary: Compile a creator's own hooks, stories and belief-shift narratives so copy carries their voice and identification.
cards.use_when: Building an ad or email angle for a store where the owner has existing content (podcasts, videos, lives).
steps: Scan several source videos and capture common sayings and phrases the owner repeats.
Pull their hooks — how they open videos and grab attention — to reuse as ad and email openers.
Identify the offer: the product or service they sell and the higher-value backend offer.
Record their 'why others are inferior' material — the critique they make of competing approaches.
Capture stories that show a belief shift; ensure any story builds identification with the audience and moves their belief.
Structure these into the copy as the story block of HSO or the justification in CJN.
For ecommerce, this keeps paid creative and email consistent with the brand owner's voice and builds trust at scale.
caveats: The source's 'belief shift' concept requires a story that genuinely changes how the reader sees the problem, not just a testimonial.

cards.title: Improve a Funnel by Improving Copy at Each Stage
cards.summary: Model the funnel as a chain (content → signup → open → buy → high-ticket) and improve the copy at every stage, not just at the buy step.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing where a store's funnel leaks — landing page signups, email opens, add-to-cart, checkout or upsell — and deciding which copy to fix first.
steps: Map each funnel stage with a realistic number: content viewers → email signups → email opens → buyers → high-ticket clients.
Identify copy-driven levers at each stage: a better subject line raises opens; better email copy raises buys; better page copy raises signups.
The source's illustrative scenario: 1M viewers, 100k signups, 10k opens, 1k book buys, 10 high-ticket buyers; improving subject lines doubled opens and book sales in the illustrative example.
Do not fix only the sale step; improving upstream copy flows through all downstream stages.
For ecommerce, adapt to ad click → PDP visit → add to cart → checkout → post-purchase upsell and fix the weakest-copy stage.
Add touch points so the brand stays top of mind; repeated seeing of a brand in email and ads increases buy probability.
caveats: The source's numeric funnel is an illustrative example, not a benchmark; substitute the store's real stage data before drawing conclusions.
Funnel math cannot distinguish copy quality from offer quality, traffic source or price.

cards.title: Use Email as a High-ROI Channel for Store Acquisition and Retention
cards.summary: Prioritize email because the source cites it as the highest-ROI marketing channel and a 40x-better acquisition tool than social alone.
cards.use_when: Deciding which channel to invest store copy effort in for acquisition, re-engagement or cart recovery.
steps: The course cites email as roughly 40 times more effective for customer acquisition than Facebook and Twitter combined; use this to justify list growth investment.
It also cites email as the highest-ROI marketing channel versus ads, SEO, direct mail and PR; use as a channel-priority argument.
Build and nurture a list of pre-qualified, opted-in prospects so a single link goes to people already interested in the niche.
Use repeated sends for top-of-mind presence even when a particular email does not drive an immediate click, because repeated exposure drives future purchases.
For ecommerce, apply to abandonment flows, replenishment and win-back programs where opted-in intent already exists.
Morning Brew is cited as an email list sold for $75 million, an example of list value, not a promise for your store.
caveats: The 40x and highest-ROI claims are the source's cited statistics; verify against current measured channel performance for the specific store.
Email success depends on list quality and deliverability, not sending frequency alone.

cards.title: Model a Launch Funnel with Copy at Each Stage (Alex Hormozi Example)
cards.summary: Use the source's worked example of a book launch funnel to see how better copy compounds through every stage to the high-ticket offer.
cards.use_when: Planning a product launch, pre-order campaign, live event or high-ticket offer funnel and deciding where copy improvements pay off most.
steps: Lay out the chain: content viewers → email signups → email opens → low-ticket purchase → high-ticket application or purchase.
Write each stage's copy to move the reader to the very next step, not straight to the final sale.
In the source's illustration, improving subject lines and email copy alone doubled low-ticket unit sales and increased high-ticket buyers, multiplying revenue.
Use the low-ticket purchase as the qualifier for the high-ticket offer; put application links or QR codes into the low-ticket product for qualified buyers.
The source cites a creator's email driving responses for a $7,000–$10,000 Mastermind, showing that copy at the email stage can drive high-ticket sales directly.
For ecommerce, mirror with a lead magnet or low-priced entry product whose insert or follow-up email routes buyers to subscription or premium tiers.
caveats: This is a worked example for illustration; the numbers are illustrative and not a promise of results.
High-ticket applications require qualification and sales capacity, not just good copy.

cards.title: Answer AI, DIY and Cheap-Hire Objections When Selling Copy
cards.summary: Anticipate the four objections SMBs raise against hiring copywriters and answer each with a concrete argument.
cards.use_when: Pitching copy services to a store owner or defending a copywriting budget during pricing discussions.
steps: AI objection: answer that AI is a tool for the writer, like a calculator for a mathematician; AI can draft an email but cannot build the marketing message and strategy.
DIY objection: business owners outsource to buy back time; they hire out video editing, sales calls and copy because their time is better spent elsewhere.

Cheap overseas hire objection: the source's position is that copy quality and care matter, and a poor fit can hurt the business more than it helps; he would rather pay $2k–$4k/month for reliable work.
Proof-of-ROI objection: if the copy makes the client tens of thousands per month, a few thousand a month is a rational trade.
Skepticism about email buyers: most people on a list have seen repeated brand messages; top-of-mind exposure drives purchases even if the person cannot recall a specific email.
Present these as the source's arguments and pair with the store's own data where possible.
caveats: These are the source's opinions for pitching, not universal truths; cheap production may be adequate for some low-stakes copy.
Do not promise specific revenue from copy without evidence from the specific store.

cards.title: Treat Business as Sales and Marketing; Copy as the Transferable Skill
cards.summary: Frame copywriting as the foundational high-income skill that unlocks marketing, funnels and other monetizable capabilities.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing which skill to build first when starting or scaling a store marketing operation.
steps: Adopt the source's framing: business is the combination of sales and marketing, and copywriting is the entry skill to both.
Build from copywriting into funnel creation, landing pages, email automation and media buying as complementary skills that raise what you can charge.
Focus on skill acquisition (get good → get money → get better → scale) rather than searching for a formula or hack.
The source argues copywriting is a more transferable version of service models like SMMA, info-product growth or growth operating, because the same skill sells any offer.
For a store operator, this means the same skill can improve ads, PDP, email and landing copy — apply it across the entire funnel, not one asset.
Use the source's progression: beginner → first client → improving skill → better clients as a long-term path.
caveats: The source presents this as a personal conviction; it is a strategic framing, not a measured business model comparison.

cards.title: Staff Copy Like an Owner: Buy Back Time with Reliable Copy
cards.summary: Small business owners outsource copy because their time is better spent elsewhere and poor work damages the brand more than it saves.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to write store copy in-house, outsource cheaply or hire a paid copywriter.
steps: Estimate the opportunity cost of the owner's time in a day versus the cost of a paid copywriter.
Assess whether cheap outsourced copy risks damaging the brand or the product's reputation; the source argues it can hurt more than help.
If the copy's expected return dwarfs the fee, paying a few thousand a month is rational.
For a store, prioritize hiring or developing copy for the highest-leverage assets first — PDP, top ad creative and core email flows.
Reinvest freed owner time into product, sourcing and growth relative to writing copy.
caveats: The source's figures — $4k/month copywriter, $2k–$4k monthly retainers — are his reported ranges, not market standards.
This is presented from the copywriter's perspective; the store operator should validate against actual returns.

cards.title: Skip Freelance Business-Building Content When Learning Copy
cards.summary: When studying copywriting for ecommerce use, filter out agency outreach scripts, personal branding and pricing/sales-call frameworks.
cards.use_when: Reviewing copywriting courses or material and deciding which modules apply to running or improving a store.
steps: Ignore freelance client outreach scripts and prospecting dialogue unless you are selling services.
Ignore social media personal branding setups aimed at freelancers, not stores.
Ignore pricing negotiations and sales-call frameworks for agency deals.
Concentrate on creative output: frameworks, mechanism, legibility, funnel copy and email structure.
Map any remaining business principles to store tasks: who writes copy, who approves it and which assets matter most.
caveats: Useful if you plan to run a copy service as a store owner or hire copywriters; skip only the freelancer-centric modules.
